title: Homework up, exams down: use AI to learn how to learn
job: Why understanding still matters when AI writes the code: Anthropic's own engineers finished faster and scored lower on mastery.
learn: The gap between output and understanding.
human: The person has to understand enough to judge the output.

title: Will capability saturate? Recursive self-improvement, and why better costs more
job: Context for the price-and-accuracy curves every agent benchmark now plots.
learn: Recursive self-improvement as an accelerant, and thinking longer as the reason better runs cost more.

title: The agent that kept deleting email: compaction dropped "confirm with me"
job: A real failure story about memory compression and safety rules.
learn: An instruction the user gave at the start was not judged important when the context was compressed.
human: Rules that must survive compaction belong outside the model's judgment.

title: Three layers: system, data, evaluation. Ask which one failed
job: A debugging frame that works in any interview: is it the system, the data, or the metric?
learn: "Choosing the wrong metric can make a weak agent look nice."

title: The most capable agent is not the most reliable
job: Reliability is the production bar. Consistency, robustness and predictability are its three measures.
learn: Princeton's finding that reliability does not track accuracy, and harness audits where safety lags completion.

title: Agents failing in the wild: a shopping agent that never asked, distraction attacks, access control
job: Stories for "how would you make an agent safe on customer data?"
learn: Operator buying milk in Iowa, pop-ups that derail agents 87% of the time, missing access control, and misalignment.
human: Knowing what the customer would have wanted asked is customer intuition, not model capability.

title: Why builders should know the model's internals
job: Knowing the KV cache and attention lets you choose the right model.
learn: Where agent builders sit on the stack.

title: Sampling and temperature
job: "Why isn't temperature 0 deterministic?" starts here.
learn: Greedy, top-k, top-p, temperature and beam search.

title: Full or linear attention: choosing a model for long context
job: A model-choice argument grounded in architecture.
learn: O(n squared) against O(n), and why linear attention forgets the needle.

title: Training models for agent work: synthetic coding tasks
job: Vocabulary for the training side of agent roles, without training models yourself.
learn: Synthetic repository tasks lifting a 32B model on SWE-bench Verified from about 9% to 40%.

title: Prefill and decode: why inference is memory-bound
job: Cost and latency questions rest on this.
learn: Compute-bound prefill, memory-bound decode, batching and speculative decoding.

title: Reasoning and inference-time scaling
job: Reasoning budgets are a cost dial you will be asked about.
learn: Thinking longer, reasoning effort settings, budget-aware training, and self-consistency as a verifier.

title: Constrained decoding and structured output
job: Structured outputs are how agents talk to code; broken JSON is a classic failure.
learn: Forcing a schema at decode time, and why it is faster and more reliable.

title: What goes into the context, the harness tax, and avoiding compaction
job: Context engineering in practice, with the Harness Tax comparison of Codex, Claude Code and Pi.
learn: System prompt, history, tools and retrieved data; ordering for the KV cache; putting the prompt in a variable instead of the window.

title: Why RAG: an answer you can check
job: The one-line motivation for retrieval.
learn: A fluent answer versus one that carries its evidence.

title: How RAG grew up, and when you need it
job: Naive, advanced and modular RAG, and the private-data case that makes retrieval necessary.
learn: Modules such as search, routing, rewrite, rerank, memory and fusion composed into patterns.

title: Chunking, contextual retrieval and hybrid search
job: The practical core of a RAG system design question.
learn: Fixed and semantic chunking, Anthropic's contextual retrieval, and combining BM25 with embeddings.

title: Hierarchical and graph RAG, chosen by cost
job: When a question needs the whole corpus, not one chunk.
learn: RAPTOR-style trees, knowledge graphs and communities, traded against retrieval quality, LLM cost and speed.

title: Measuring retrieval: hit@k, nDCG, recall@k
job: You will be asked how you would know retrieval works.
learn: What each metric rewards, and training the retriever on more data.

title: Agentic RAG, and is RAG out of date?
job: Agentic RAG is the current form, and "is RAG dead?" is a live interview question.
learn: Self-RAG, corrective RAG, search agents trained with RL, and the risks: compounding errors and injection.

title: How RAG fails, and lost in the middle
job: RAG appears in two-thirds of harness postings; its failure list is interview material.
learn: Permission leaks, distraction, conflicting evidence, injection, and the U-shaped accuracy curve over document position.

title: Citations can be hallucinated too
job: Grounding is not proven by a citation. Know the numbers.
learn: Users rate generative search highly while citation precision and recall stay low.

title: Change the tool description, not the model: REST, function calling, MCP
job: MCP is a named must-have. This is the history that explains why it exists.
learn: Three generations: docs for humans, JSON schemas for models, a protocol for an ecosystem.

title: How MCP works, and who gets which tools
job: Production MCP is about permissions as much as tools. This covers hosts, clients, servers and access control.
learn: tools/list and tools/call, FastMCP, and a course server that gates who may post grades while neither side sees the other's token.
human: Who may call which tool is a policy a person sets.

title: Building an agent versus engineering one, and the framework map
job: Places LangGraph, DSPy, Temporal and observability tools on one map.
learn: You can build without data or evals; you cannot engineer without them.

title: LangGraph in five minutes: state, nodes, edges
job: LangGraph is named in about a third of harness postings and as a must-have in some.
learn: Shared state, nodes that read and write it, edges for control flow, and why a graph helps retries and observability.

title: Conditional edges, LangGraph agents, and LangGraph versus DSPy
job: The comparison question you will be asked, answered by someone who uses both.
learn: Routing functions, create_agent, different models per node, and composing DSPy inside LangGraph.

title: Durable execution with Temporal, and observability tools
job: Reliability, durable execution and observability are production must-haves; Temporal, LangSmith and Langfuse are the names.
learn: Retries under a flaky worker shown in Temporal's history; what LangSmith and Langfuse show you.

title: Best practices: keep it simple, make failures observable, build the eval first
job: Close to a checklist of what agent-engineering job descriptions ask for.
learn: Workflows before agents, trace everything, retries and timeouts, meta-agents that watch, and evals on your own domain rather than public benchmarks.
human: Choosing the metric and the representative cases is the person's work.

title: The cost of frameworks: show me the prompt
job: A mature answer to "would you use a framework?": dependencies, longevity, and knowing what runs underneath.
learn: Abstractions hide failures; look at the traces.

title: Workflow or agent: where the control flow lives
job: "Do you know when not to use an agent?" Workflows are predictable; agents are adaptable and harder to evaluate.
learn: The predictability and agency trade-off, with a support-ticket example of each.
human: Choosing how much control to hand the model is a design decision about risk.

title: Five workflow patterns: chain, route, parallelize, orchestrate, evaluate-optimize
job: Anthropic's "Building effective agents" taxonomy is a standard system-design vocabulary.
learn: Each pattern with what it trades: latency for accuracy, cost-aware routing to small models, guardrails run in parallel, and when an evaluator loop is worth it.

title: Self-reflection often makes it worse; external verifiers help
job: The "ask it to check its own work" trap, with the paper that answers it.
learn: "Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet", and CRITIC: a verifier with tools beats self-review.

title: CodeAct: code as the action
job: Tool-call design comes up in harness interviews; code-as-action wins on success and turns.
learn: One program with loops and min() instead of a dozen JSON tool calls.

title: Context engineering: keep it focused, keep it continuous
job: Prompt and context engineering appears in four of ten harness postings.
learn: Lost in the middle, keeping only what the task needs, and preserving goals, constraints and the KV cache.

title: Keep a persistent event log
job: The design behind auditability and observability in production agents.
learn: OpenHands rebuilds every prompt from a full event stream, so compaction never loses the record and hooks can observe.

title: Compaction or observation masking
job: A scenario question waiting to happen: context is too long, what do you drop?
learn: Observations are most of the tokens; masking them is simpler than summarizing and about as good, with KV-cache trade-offs.

title: Context isolation: sub-agents, skills and progressive disclosure
job: How skills differ from tools, a question people get wrong.
learn: Sub-agents flood their own context and report back; skills list names up front and load contents on demand.

title: Pi, the minimal harness: strong models need simple harnesses, weak ones need better ones
job: Harness engineering in one sentence, and the safety cost of having no permission prompts.
learn: Four default tools, an event-log tree, skills, compaction, no safeguards, and why it works anyway.
human: "The best models need a very simple harness, but bad models need better harnesses." Deciding how much harness a model needs is a measured judgment.

title: Why agents need memory
job: Context layers and customer memory are named in agent postings. This is the problem statement.
learn: Lost procedure, lost knowledge, lost progress; personalization, learning from experience, statefulness.

title: Four kinds of memory: working, episodic, semantic, procedural
job: The vocabulary an interviewer expects when you describe a memory system.
learn: The context window is working memory; logs are episodic; facts are semantic; skill files are procedural.

title: When memories conflict, and when memory belongs in the weights
job: A good follow-up answer: context usually overrides weights; facts go in context, skills can go in weights.
learn: Why fine-tuning facts needs thousands of documents and is lossy, while RL on a task can improve procedure.

title: Often the best memory is just a file system
job: The simple answer that strong models make possible, and the trade-off (latency).
learn: Set up the simplest thing and let the model run the show; reach for fancier systems only for a reason.

title: Skills as procedural memory: Voyager's skill library
job: Skills, the format Claude Code and others now use, have a research lineage. Know it.
learn: Write code for a task, keep it if the environment confirms success, retrieve it by description later.

title: On MemoryArena, the memory agents scored worst
job: Evidence that "add a memory system" is not automatically better. Measure it.
learn: Long context, memory agents and RAG compared on group travel planning with growing constraints.

title: Open problems in memory: what to keep, poisoned memories, privacy, over-personalization
job: An agent that remembers customer data needs answers to exactly these questions.
learn: Ambiguous things to remember, memory injection attacks, leaking private context, and the model that over-uses what it remembers.
human: What should be remembered, and what must never be shared, is a call about the customer that a person makes.

title: What multi-agent buys you, and what it costs
job: Multi-agent orchestration is a named requirement. Know the benefits and the five drawbacks.
learn: Parallelism, specialization and isolated context against coordination overhead, information loss, conflicting actions, error propagation and complexity.

title: One agent often beats many: start with a strong single-agent baseline
job: The trap interviewers set is "add more agents". Google's scaling study says single agents often win.
learn: When to prefer one agent (dependent steps, coupled work, already good enough) and when to try many (parallel, divisible work).
human: Deciding whether the work divides is a judgment about the task, made before any agent runs.

title: Who decides to spawn sub-agents, and why it always costs more
job: Cost and latency show up in a third of harness postings. Every sub-agent reloads the whole context.
learn: Today you still have to tell a coding agent to fan out; multi-agent almost always costs more than single-agent.

title: The architecture depends on the task, and so does the bill
job: A one-minute answer to "which orchestration pattern?": it depends on the task, and the cost ladder runs single, orchestrator, swarm.
learn: Decentralized agents won on finance documents and fell apart on planning tasks.

title: Why multi-agent systems fail
job: Failure modes are what scenario interviews are made of.
learn: The failure taxonomy (system design, inter-agent misalignment, verification) and CooperBench's expectation, commitment and communication failures.

title: Swarms that all build ray tracers, and one that kicks the others off
job: A memorable safety story for an interview about agents acting with permissions.
learn: Conformity (no diversity of thought) and conflicting goals settled by force, passivity or truce.

title: Is prompt work still needed? Last-mile adaptation
job: A common interview question: "won't better models make this unnecessary?" Here is a defensible answer.
learn: The three pillars (system, data, metric), and context optimization as last-mile adaptation rather than fiddling with wording.

title: When to optimize: evals carry intent you could not write down
job: Explains when automatic optimization pays: reliability, domain fit, cheaper models, and re-optimizing when a new model ships.
learn: Examples and feedback communicate requirements a prompt leaves out.
human: Your taste and hidden requirements get into the system through the eval set.

title: Agents that rewrite their own harness: meta-harness and autoresearch
job: Harness engineering pointed at itself. Know the meta-harness and autoresearch ideas by name.
learn: An agent proposing, running and keeping or reverting its own changes, scored on Terminal-Bench.
human: "The metric and eval become the most critical part to control." When the AI improves the AI, the person owns the metric.

title: Prompts or weights: how to choose
job: A crisp decision list for the "fine-tune or prompt?" question.
learn: Context optimization for API models, frequent re-runs and expensive rollouts; weights for small models, distillation and contexts that keep growing.

title: Outputs are the new source of truth
job: Every harness posting asks for evaluation. This is the argument for why: generated code is judged by what it does, not by reading it.
learn: Chollet's point that agentic coding is a form of machine learning, and the shift of the developer's job from specifying toward evaluating.
human: The person's work moves from writing the program to deciding what correct looks like.

title: Writing an eval task: the instruction and the environment
job: "Every agent you own has an eval suite" is a must-have in agent roles. This is how Terminal-Bench writes one task.
learn: Fully specified, concise, natural instructions; environments that match production; internet access as a trade-off; baking state in to cut flakiness.

title: Verifiers are the hardest part, and reward hacking
job: Interviewers probe evals that agents game. This names the defences: one-to-one requirement coverage, separate verifier containers, judges that are themselves evaluated.
learn: A verifier is a classifier with false positives and negatives; model-based verifiers trade away determinism; reward hacking never ends.

title: Where a person has the most leverage: the verifier's decision boundary
job: The best answer to "what do you bring when the AI writes the code?": you decide what passes.
learn: Offline evals from online observation, why one observed example is one data point, and why a little human work on a verifier pays across thousands of trials.
human: "This job of the evaluator is probably the point of highest leverage for people." A health-care front desk is the student's example.

title: Publish the traces, not a score
job: Observability and honest reporting: agent behaviour is high-dimensional, and a single score hides reward hacks and slop.
learn: Why the community found reward hacks and bloated code only because full traces were released.
